chapters.title: Applicant Walker-Stewart on Sojourner site unit mix and affordability

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So this is the first floor plan with the amenities flanking the lobby and then the single entry in the lobby as well as the maisonettes in blue.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Which we'll look at the second floor plan.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: You can see the second story of the maisonettes and then we're introducing the one bedrooms, two bedrooms, three bedrooms as well.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So this is the preliminary unit distribution and affordability mix.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Just want to highlight here that we're creating over 60% of our units as two bedrooms and three bedrooms as we recognize that family size units are very important to this community.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And then for the affordability range, we're providing our space units set aside at 15%, and then we have a range of affordability from 30% AMI to 80% AMI.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So this highlights the diversity of units and households that we are hoping to house.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.text: So this is the second phase of the project, the MAPES court site.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: As Matthew mentioned, this is an existing FIPS building that has existing tenants that will be, once the Sojourner site is built, relocated.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Their relocation costs will be covered by FIPS.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: They will retain...

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Phipps acquired those sites in order to redevelop it and create brand new more affordable units to this corner.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart

chapters.summary: Walker-Stewart presents the MAPES building: 298 affordable units, 6-14 stories, over 15,000 sq ft of community space potentially for a YMCA, with massing concentrated on wide streets and stepping down to residential streets. She notes a meeting with YMCA is scheduled.
chapters.title: Applicant Walker-Stewart on MAPES building design and community space

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So we are hoping to create 298 units of affordable housing with the same residential amenity space on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: The project ranges in height between 6 and 14 stories.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Again, the massing response to the street corners, concentrating the height on the wide street, and then stepping down to the residential.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: streets.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: What sets this building apart from Sojourner and what we're really excited about is that we are creating over 15,000 square feet of community space and we know the council member has been interested in using the space for a community center,

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: he's expressed interest in YMCA and so we wanted to let you know where you're meeting with them tomorrow to discuss the feasibility of that.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: This is another perspective showing that distribution of massing and urban design sensitivity and the community facility space on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: You can see again, we're stepping down to Mapes Avenue, which is a real residential street.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So again, we're being sensitive to the neighborhood context.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So this is the first floor plan.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: In white, you can see the community facility space.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And then the middle, this MAPES court would also have a landscaped area for tenants.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: A single point of entry lobby.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: This is a security measure as well as tenants will be greeted by concierge.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And then in blue, we introduce residential units along MAPES Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide.

chapters.summary: Walker-Stewart presents the MAPES unit mix: 55% two and three bedrooms (nearly double the city's 30% minimum), affordability from 30% to 80% AMI, designed to house diverse households including teachers and families.
chapters.title: Applicant Walker-Stewart on MAPES unit mix and affordability range

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: This is the second to sixth floor plan.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Next slide.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And this is the preliminary unit distribution and affordability mix for MAPES.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Similarly to Sojourner, we have a very high concentration of two bedrooms and three bedrooms, 55%.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: For context, the city requires a 30% minimum, and we are doubling it for both, or practically doubling it for MAPES.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And similarly, next slide.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: We are looking to create a diverse range of affordability levels.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So we are creating homes for teachers and their family of three, making around 75K, two architects making around 90K.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: We appreciate your time.

utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Felice, and I wanted to give him an opportunity to provide remarks.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Feliz thanks Phipps for their work in the Bronx, looks forward to building needed housing and resolving local community issues including youth needs, and defers questions to the chair.
chapters.title: Council Member Feliz remarks on Sojourner Truth MAPES

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I just want to thank you all for the presentation and for all the work that you do in the Central and the South Bronx, building affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Look forward to working together on this, making sure that this is a project that is able to build the housing that we need in our city, but also help resolve some of the local issues in the community, including the needs, especially that our youth have in the area.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I have some questions, but I'll let the chair go first with the questions.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Chair Louis asks how the project achieves a high percentage of family-sized units. Kelly Biscuso explains the scale allows Phipps to design buildings they believe in with larger units, and Matthew Washington adds that Phipps is mission-driven and owns/manages buildings long-term.
chapters.title: Chair Louis questions on achieving high percentage of family-sized units

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Two quick questions, and I'll hand it over to Councilmember Felice.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: The project would have a larger number of two to three bedrooms, as you just mentioned, than most 100% affordable housing applications that come through this committee.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Can you explain how you were able to accomplish this goal?

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: Thank you for picking up on that.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: I mean, it's something we pride ourselves in at FIPS is that we, in part, by trying to build at this scale, it allows us to try and design the buildings we really believe in.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: So to be able to staff a concierge at the front desk, to be able to have larger units.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And so we've, I think in part, having the scale, having the experience we do, we've definitely proven out on previous projects we've done recently that we can accommodate that amount of bedroom sizes.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And we really are aiming to build housing for families.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: larger units than typical.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: So I think it's part of our track record, part of our model, and part of how we design buildings from the inception.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: So it's part of why we're putting this proposal in front of you today to be able to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And Chair Lewis, if I may add, you know, we're a mission-driven organization, and we know that there's a need for housing for families.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: When you look at the financing models, a lot of them are looking at unit count and don't really distinguish between a studio or a three-bedroom or a two-bedroom when you're looking at the financing, but it's important for us to push because of the communities that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: You know, we're not a developer who builds buildings and runs away.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: We own and manage our buildings and have been doing so since the 19, we still have one of our buildings since 1931 that we're still managing today.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so it's important to us that we are serving the communities that we're a part of.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And it's also why we build community centers in these neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And we're building a new community center, not far from this project here on 180th Street and Boston Road, but it's serving and it's really pushing on that mission to make a difference in the lives of the people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Very noble.

chapters.summary: Chair Louis asks why the R8 rezoning is necessary when large buildings could be built as-of-right. Washington explains as-of-right yields ~300 units vs. ~460 with rezoning, and the additional scale supports community facility space, amenities, and family-sized units. Walker-Stewart adds the scale enables 62% family units.
chapters.title: Chair Louis questions on why R8 rezoning is necessary

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: The community board mentioned that large apartment buildings could be built on these lots without any rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Can you explain why a rezoning is necessary and why the R8 zoning district was selected?

utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.text: Ashley, do you want?

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: I can start.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: Ashley will pick up on it.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: I mean, so as of right, you could probably build about 300 units.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: on the site.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And our project contemplates about 460, you know, close to that.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so there are a couple of reasons.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: One, there's a need for affordable housing in the city.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so being able to do that is important.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: Plus, it allows us to, you know, increase the scale that allows for the incorporation of the community facility space, you know, beautification of the area around it.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: You know, one of the things that's important with the rezoning and as we went through environmental review, there is a community garden across the street from the Sojourner Truth site, which was of interest to the community board, you know.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: With hopefully the approval of the city council, we'll be paying for a redesign to address any concerns about shadows that the community garden has.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And we've already been in touch with Green Thumb and to talk with them about the process.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so a lot of it is understanding the needs that the city has, building to a scale that can support things like

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: the amenity spaces we want to provide for residents, such as concierge, making sure that families can receive packages that don't grow legs and walk away, which unfortunately happens sometimes in buildings.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so being able to provide a suite of amenities, you really just need more income to make it work.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so it's what really finances and functions for our properties.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And Kelly mentioned this earlier, but I just want to emphasize.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: The scale of the building allows us to create the 62% family size units.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: If we were to reduce the scale of the building, we wouldn't be able to support that.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And we recognize that it's an important part of that.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: It's an important.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: Request from the community that we create more family size units and we had conversations with the borough president that this is a priority for her so we're we're excited we're able to do that because of because of the scale of the project right

chapters.summary: Council Member Feliz asks about shadows on the community garden. Washington reports Phipps has been in touch with Green Thumb and committed to funding a redesign of the Hornaday Community Garden to address shadow concerns upon project approval.
chapters.title: Council Member Feliz questions on community garden shadow remedies

utterances.text: thank you councilman felice thank you again chair and thank you again all for being here

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A few questions about the project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think anybody who's been paying attention to me knows how I feel about green spaces, the need to build green spaces, preserve them, and also make them accessible.

chapters.title: Council Member Feliz questions on Crotona Parkway mall shadows

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington

utterances.text: They're excited about the opportunity to do that because, you know, we wouldn't want to have that.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: negative impacts, and they're excited about the potential of residents, more residents, becoming members of the garden as well.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: So we've certainly had conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What about the Cortona Parkway malls, the green strip that runs right in front of the area of Southern Boulevard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Would this cast a shadow on that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if yes, how much?

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: Patrick, do you want to?

utterances.speaker: Patrick Blanchfield
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Patrick Blanchfield
utterances.text: So the project would cast shadows, some shadows on the Cortona Park malls, but the extent and the duration is minimal, such that it wouldn't really rise to any kind of significance,

utterances.speaker: Patrick Blanchfield
utterances.text: but it would cast a little bit of shadow, but nothing that would...

utterances.speaker: Patrick Blanchfield
utterances.text: Nothing that would rise to a significant impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks how the project fits the neighborhood context given most buildings are lower. Architect Magnus Westergren says the 100-foot-wide Southern Boulevard supports 14 stories. Walker-Stewart notes only ~25% of the building is at maximum height, with the majority at 8-10 stories. Washington adds taller slimmer buildings cast shorter shadows than short squat structures.
chapters.title: Council Member Feliz questions on building height and neighborhood context

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the community board has mentioned many things, including the fact that the height seems out of context with the rest of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are a few towers, including 21 at Evans on the Boulevard, 30 stories, also 800 East 180th and 820.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But that's only a few buildings out of the many buildings that are in the area, including right next to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So just curious, what makes this project fit within the context of the surrounding neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And why not bring it a little bit down so that it could be a little closer to everything around the building?

utterances.speaker: Magnus Westergren
utterances.text: I mean, I think given the width of Southern Boulevard and Cortona Parkway, you know, it's an extremely expansive street.

utterances.speaker: Magnus Westergren

utterances.speaker: Magnus Westergren
utterances.text: So given that, it seemed that 14 stories was a good height, you know, in terms of the scale of the street to the building.

utterances.speaker: Magnus Westergren
utterances.text: And then obviously the height, again, echoes the family unit sizes and the overall number of units for it.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: And the...

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: While the tallest point, the tallest height of the building is 14 stories, let's say on Mapes Avenue, it only makes up less than a quarter of the rest of the building.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So the majority of the building is 10 stories and 8 stories, as well as Sojourner's side is less than, I think like 44% is actually at the 16.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: So the end.

utterances.speaker: Astrid Walker-Stewart
utterances.text: As Magnus mentioned, we worked with his very thoughtful architecture team, and they were very thoughtful about where to place that height and how important step downs are and setbacks are.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And just relate to that council member, you know, one of the things that's important, and Magnus and Patrick can certainly speak more to this, but by having that, you still allow more light to come in.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: And so if you have sort of a short squat structure, it casts a bigger, longer shadow over those places that we're trying to protect and allow light and air to come into.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: So that's an important part as well.

utterances.speaker: Magnus Westergren
utterances.text: Yeah, I will add just the size of the courtyards are also, that's the way that we can maintain pretty large at-grade courtyard spaces, you know, green spaces, is by making the building a little bit slimmer and a little bit taller in places.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington
utterances.text: Well, we would likely lose units if we expanded it beyond what it is at this point.

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington

utterances.speaker: Matthew Washington

utterances.text: I could just ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: So if the community, I know we're debating the height of the building and the rezoning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If the community agreed to allow even taller housing,

utterances.text: But obviously a challenge within the city when they do these is they expect those spaces to sort of fully fund themselves through rent.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And, you know, when you start talking about a 20,000, 30,000 square foot space.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: You obviously don't want to just end up with a vacant space that the city's not going to fund.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And so it's really trying to find that sweet spot.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And so as mentioned, we're having those exploratory conversations to figure out what the right space is.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: But it is something we'd have to explore and figure out with the city.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: There would need to obviously be council support.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: And there would need to be a partner who could actually, that it would work for.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Biscuso
utterances.text: So that's really the piece that we're...

utterances.text: In particular related to the size question.

utterances.text: Okay, and final question.

utterances.text: Talk to us about the labor aspect of this.

utterances.text: We do have a CBA in place at MAPES Court today, and even the Sojourner Truth site, Astra during the presentation showed that it was a vacant site.

chapters.summary: Rafael Moure-Punnett, district manager for Bronx Community Board 6, explains the board voted no because Phipps can build 300 units as-of-right without rezoning. He argues the council should only reward responsible developers with discretionary rezoning, citing federal class action lawsuits and high housing code violations at Phipps properties.
chapters.title: Public testimony: Rafael Moure-Punnett (CB6) explains board's no vote on Phipps track record

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: Thank you, council members, for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: My name is Rafael Mori-Pinette.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: The community board voted no on the sojourner Mavis pre-zoning, and I wanted to clarify some of the points made by the board in our letter to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: Community Board 6, this area is an area where a lot of as-of-right development happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: There are regularly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: Tall buildings built out of houses that are combined in multiple lots into one new building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: As a result, Community Board 6 has a very active development market, and we are doing more than our fair share of new housing construction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: for the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: This rezoning, this discretionary rezoning before the council is not going to make or break the real estate market in our district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: And we have encouraged the council to vote no on this because we know that FIPS can still build 300 units on this law without a rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: And we believe that the city council should really only reward responsible developers with rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: A developer that doesn't have a good track record in a neighborhood is not a good candidate for discretionary rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: The board hears from, on a regular basis,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: many FIPS tenants, including a tenant last night at our Housing and Land Use Committee, with serious concerns about FIPS's management practices, some of which have been brought up today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: And, you know, FIPS tenants organized and a federal class action lawsuit was filed against FIPS, alleging these

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: management practices that cause severe harm to the tenants, whether they're repairs, rent recertification, or things of that nature, the buildings in this rezoning area are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: referred to in our letter as having high housing code violations and serious

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rafael Moure-Punnett
utterances.text: problems for the tenants in that area.

chapters.summary: Brigette Brantley, a Bronx resident and community advocate, asks how Phipps can ask for new development when they haven't fixed existing problems. She questions who the development is for, given it's one of the poorest congressional districts, and urges council members to listen to constituents over developers.
chapters.title: Public testimony: Brigette Brantley demands accountability before new development

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: So I have to ask, who is this development really for?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: Development in the Bronx should benefit the people who already live in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: And before we talk about rezoning and expansion, deal with the complaints, deal with the violations, deal with the repairs, deal with the tenants asking to be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: And to every city council member listening, whether you represent my district or not, I hope you hear me loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: Listen to the constituents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley
utterances.text: This is about accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brigette Brantley

summary: The Subcommittee on Zoning and Franchises voted 7-0 (later 8-0) to approve three rezoning proposals: 815 Hutchinson River Parkway (Bronx), 862-868 Kent Avenue (Brooklyn), and 132 Melrose Street (Brooklyn) with a modification removing MIH Option 2.

The subcommittee held hearings on six pre-considered rezoning applications: Park Avenue Brooklyn, 289 Kent Avenue, Fort Hamilton Mews (Bay Ridge), 21-31 46th Avenue (LIC), 69-67 108th Street (Forest Hills), and Sojourner Truth MAPES (Bronx), with extensive public testimony on several.

Key themes included concerns about neighborhood character and infrastructure capacity (LIC, Bay Ridge), labor agreements with 32BJ (Fort Hamilton Mews, Sojourner Truth MAPES), Phipps Houses' management track record (Sojourner Truth MAPES), and the impact of new charter changes limiting council authority over rezoning decisions.
